source.title: AutomaTikZ: Text-Guided Synthesis of Scientific Vector Graphics with TikZ
source.authors: Jonas Belouadi; Anne Lauscher; S. Eger

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares task performance for 7b and 13b fine-tuned models on a held-out set, using task-specific metrics rather than pretraining loss or a scaling-law fit.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-size comparisons for TikZ generation, which bear on V6. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit scaling laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or compare compute-optimal allocations. Its comparisons of LLaMA and CLiMA are not tests of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
record.test_reason: This is an application paper on TikZ generation. It fine-tunes LLaMA and CLiMA at two sizes (7b, 13b) with LoRA and reports task metrics. It cites Kaplan et al. only to frame the 13b-over-7b result as expected. Two sizes of LoRA-tuned models on one task cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale. There is no fit, no trend across scale, and no link to pretraining loss. It also measures no pretraining loss, fits no laws, and tests no allocation or shape. So it bears on no version. The size comparison is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but imprecise. The authors say the 13b models clearly beat the 7b models on all string-similarity and image-based metrics, by 0.2–0.5pp, with CSR comparable. They present this as matching the intuitive expectation from Kaplan et al. They do not discuss the CLiMA CER reversal. Their main conclusions concern CLiMA beating LLaMA, GPT-4 and Claude 2, and typographic attacks; scaling is not among them.
record.recipe_differences: This is a fine-tuning and held-out task-evaluation comparison between 7b and 13b models, not a language-model pretraining scaling-law experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 3 compares LoRA-fine-tuned 13b and 7b models on TikZ generation. The 13b models score better on EED, KID, CLIPScore_img, CLIPScore and CrystalBLEU for both LLaMA and CLiMA, by small margins. CSR is comparable across sizes. CER improves for LLaMA but worsens for CLiMA (0.545 to 0.656).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger fine-tuned LLMs (13b vs 7b) do modestly better on most metrics of a niche code-generation task, but not on compilability.

record.problems: Only two parameter sizes are compared, and both model families are fine-tuned for one task. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the automatic metric comparisons.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss measured, no power-law fit.
All: no extrapolation from small runs.
All: no depth/width variation at fixed parameter count; CLiMA adds a CLIP adapter, which is not a shape change.
All: no scaling fit in any modality or regime.
Predictability with scale or pretraining loss. Only two sizes are compared, with no trend fit and no loss measured.
All: no exponents or fitting choices examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'tested' call and its labels are dropped. Two model sizes, fine-tuned with LoRA on frozen half-precision base weights, give no information about whether downstream performance scales predictably. Kaplan et al. is cited once, as framing. Row values were checked against Table 3 and are correct.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss over parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations across compute budgets.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether scaling-law forms hold in other modalities or training regimes.

The study tests task-specific held-out TikZ generation after fine-tuning at two model sizes only. It does not test predictability across a wide scale range, other downstream tasks, or the relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and possible curve bending.
